Ep 34: A mile of subway can cost two billion dollars in one city and a tenth that in another, even with similar rock and water tables, because the raw materials and boring hours explain almost none of the difference.
Ep 36: Cement that binds our buildings costs many times the limestone and fuel alone, because the century-old kiln process itself is the real expense.
Ep 35: Copper cables costing thousands per kilometer gave way to glass strands worth pennies once engineers treated data movement as a purity problem instead of a wiring problem.
Ep 40: A package can cross an ocean for pennies per kilogram, yet the last few kilometers to a doorstep often multiply the total cost several times over.
Ep 37: Intricate patterned cloth once demanded teams of skilled hands per row; punched cards collapsed that labor into the cost of thread and a stack of holes.
Ep 42: A ton of old circuit boards already contains more gold than a ton of virgin ore, yet the cost to recover it still sits many times higher than the metals themselves.
Ep 41: Ice once cut from frozen ponds and hauled across oceans now costs pennies to produce anywhere because engineers asked what it truly takes to pump heat out of a box.
Ep 38: A routine dental filling can cost hundreds while the materials inside are worth only a few dollars, showing where the real price drivers sit.

Ep 54: The 1968 National Flood Insurance Program set out to limit building in flood-prone areas but instead subsidized far more development behind levees.
Ep 55: US dietary guidelines urged Americans to cut fat for heart health — and watched obesity climb as sugar filled the gap.
Ep 58: Companies adopted game mechanics to make fitness, learning, and work more engaging — and watched users chase points while real progress and well-being declined.
Ep 59: The U.S. government paid southern farmers to plant kudzu to stop erosion — and the vine kept growing long after the crisis ended.
Ep 57: Twentieth-century engineers built dams to power the West and control floods, then spent decades dismantling some so salmon could reach their spawning grounds again.
